title: Teaching
text: I view teaching and research as deeply interconnected, with both grounded in curiosity, rigor, and collaboration. In the classroom, I encourage students to apply social science theories to their own experiences, fostering critical thinking and a sense of ownership. My goal is to create an inclusive environment where students from all backgrounds feel empowered to contribute, grow, and see themselves as part of the scholarly community.

title: Teaching
text:
Research Mentorship
In Spring 2026, I led the Belief Systems Lab’s undergraduate research program while my advisor was on research leave, helping guide student teams through every stage of the research process. My teams took first, second, and third place in their section at Michigan State’s University Undergraduate Research and Arts Forum (UURAF).

First place, best research presentation in psychology. “To what extent does your social group (or ‘close others’) agree or disagree with your political views?” — Genevieve Orlewicz, Nicole Thomas, & Peyton McLaughlin
Second place, best research presentation in psychology. “Does your social group influence how open you are to differing political views?” — Genevieve Orlewicz, Nicole Thomas, & Peyton McLaughlin
Third place, best research presentation in psychology. “The relationship between religion and media trust” — Emma Dye
“How country pride affects immigrants’ life satisfaction” — Madeline Hilditch & Mina Arikan

I also mentor undergraduates as collaborators on manuscripts, and have published with student collaborators as lead authors. I look forward to continuing this collaborative, student centric approach as faculty.

Welcome to my website! I’m a Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Belief Identity and Group Relations Lab at the University of Illinois Chicago. I completed my PhD in Social & Personality Psychology at Michigan State University in 2026, following an MA in Political Science at UNC Chapel Hill. I study beliefs and belief-system dynamics. Specifically, my research asks why individuals vary in the content and meta-cognitive properties of their beliefs, and what societal implications the content and meta-cognitive properties of beliefs may have.
I address my central research questions with three interrelated lines:

individual differences and belief dynamics. I examine how individual differences shape the content, organization, and evolution of beliefs.
belief stability and change in context. I test when and why beliefs and their meta-cognitive properties (e.g., moral conviction, extremity) change or remain the same when socio-political circumstances shift.
belief change interventions contextualized. I question the consequences of belief change interventions in context, and when it makes sense to maximize epistemically grounded belief change versus raw persuasion.

Across these strands, I emphasize rigorous open-science, comprehensive evidence, and collaboration. My work has been recognized with the 2025 SPSP Student Publication Award and supported by the Institute for Humane Studies. I am also deeply committed to mentoring student researchers as collaborators.
